expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
expectations.evidence: The opening rejects silence and asks for a budget: 'Close the same-role gap within two to three pay rounds, tell your people and the works council what you found, and give the CFO a costed budget instead of a five-year drift.' But the plan is never dated. No pay round has a calendar date or month, and 'Write a dated plan' is left to the user. Two to three annual rounds ('Higher in years 1 to 3, then done') can run to about three years, which isn't much faster than five.

expectations.text: The reply states correctly that equal pay for equal work is already law (Article 157 TFEU or national equal pay law), so a same-role gap is a legal exposure now, whatever the transposition date of the new directive.
expectations.evidence: 'Equal pay is already law. Equal pay for equal work is already required (Article 157 TFEU, plus Dutch and Belgian national law). A 6% gap in the same role and grade is an exposure today, whatever the date of the new transparency rules.'

expectations.text: The reply gets the EU Pay Transparency Directive right: a gap of 5% or more within a category of workers that can't be justified by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months triggers a joint pay assessment with workers' representatives; and it notes at least one of the reporting thresholds and dates, the employee right to information, or that transposition is late (the Dutch law is expected in 2027).
expectations.evidence: 'If a gap of 5% or more in a category of workers can't be explained by objective, gender-neutral factors and isn't fixed within six months, you must carry out a joint pay assessment with employee representatives.' Also: 'the Dutch bill puts the first report on 7 June 2028' (correct) and 'Employees will also be able to ask for pay averages by sex for their own role.' It later contradicts itself with '2027 report' (see factual_errors), but its account of the directive is right.

expectations.text: The reply separates the overall gap from the same-role gap and explains how to analyse what objective factors explain, with care for small groups.
expectations.evidence: Separates the gaps ('The 14% overall gap is a different problem, about who sits in which roles and grades'). Method: 'run again in code, by country, and show how many people sit in each role and grade cell. Groups under five are reported only in aggregate. Separate what objective factors explain... from what they don't. Also check that your grades are not carrying the gap.'

expectations.text: The reply puts a number on the cost of closing the same-role gap, or shows how to compute it from the payroll data, and frames it for the CFO against the cost of claims, attrition or reputation.
expectations.evidence: 'If 130 women are on an average of EUR 70,000 and the unexplained gap is 6%, the fix is roughly EUR 550,000 a year. Spread over two or three pay rounds, that is roughly EUR 180,000 to 275,000 extra a round' (130 x 70k x 6% = 546k). 'The CFO should compare that with the cost of a claim, back pay, losing people (replacing an engineer costs half to two times salary) and a public report.'

expectations.text: The reply includes telling employees or their representatives honestly and fixing the causes (such as starting pay, promotion or bonus decisions).
expectations.evidence: 'Brief the works council and Belgian employee representatives first, while the plan can still change. Then tell all employees what you found, what you will do and by when, and how they can ask about their own pay.' Causes: 'Set starting-salary rules so offers aren't negotiated case by case. Give bonus and promotion decisions written criteria. Check part-time and leave effects.'

overall_quality.evidence: Sound on the core law, with good small-group and grading-bias checks and a usable CFO line. But it has no dates, a two-to-three-round pace that undercuts its own urgency, no per-entity or Belgian 2012-act detail, and a '2027 report' claim that contradicts its own correct 2028 date.

factual_errors.evidence: 1) To the CFO: 'from 2027 we have to report', and the risk list names 'a public report in 2027' and 'the 2027 report'. But the reply itself correctly says 'the Dutch bill puts the first report on 7 June 2028', and Belgium has no date yet, so no report is due in 2027. Also imprecise but not counted: 'With 650 employees you fall in the group that reports every year' ignores that reporting is per employer, so a Belgian entity of 230 would report every three years.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: No leader says the gap is leadership's responsibility.

best_insight.value: Check that the grades aren't carrying the gap, because women may have been graded lower for similar work, so the role-and-grade 6% can understate the problem.

suggestions.assertion: The reply separates the overall gap from the same-role gap and explains how to analyse what objective factors explain, with care for small groups.
suggestions.reason: The clause 'with care for small groups' decides this assertion: B, C, F and G give strong analysis methods (hourly pay, all pay elements, equal-value comparisons, testing whether the controls are biased) and still fail on it. Consider splitting it into (a) separating the gaps and the objective-factor method and (b) small-cell handling, so the score shows which part was missed.

No assertion checks the Belgian side, although it is what most defeats the CFO's 'say nothing' plan: the 22 April 2012 pay gap act already requires a pay-structure analysis for the works council every two years (50+ workers). It also doesn't check per-entity scope (Dutch entity 420 = annual reporting; Belgian 230 = 150-249 band). The strongest samples covered both.

suggestions.assertion: The reply opens with a recommendation to close the same-role gap on a dated, budgeted plan much faster than five years, and not to keep it quiet.
suggestions.reason: 'Opens with ... a dated, budgeted plan' is ambiguous about whether the dates and budget must appear in the opening or anywhere in the reply. Only H puts both in its first lines. Say which is meant.

Nothing checks whether the reply warns against funding the corrections from colleagues' raises or merit budget, or whether leadership owns the cause. Both separate good advice from merely compliant advice here (B suggests using part of the merit budget; C and H warn against it; E and H put the leadership bonus pool first).

eval_feedback.overall: Strong on law and analysis, but the one sample with no dates at all, and its pace (two to three rounds) is the slowest recommended.
